round.title: One parity round of the 3-qubit bit-flip code
round.idea: Two parity checks, a decode on the decoder core and a frame update on the frame core: every kind of system call a round needs.
round.source:
# One round of the 3-qubit bit-flip code: two parity checks, a decode, a frame update.
# Data qubits data[0:2]; two ancillas; no statement carries a time: the OS schedules them.
request_ancilla  count=2  ancilla[0:1]
route  ancilla[0], data[0:1]
CNOT  data[0], ancilla[0]
CNOT  data[1], ancilla[0]
route  ancilla[1], data[1:2]
CNOT  data[1], ancilla[1]
CNOT  data[2], ancilla[1]
measure  basis=Z  ancilla[0] -> s[0]
measure  basis=Z  ancilla[1] -> s[1]
release_ancilla  count=2  ancilla[0:1]
s[0:1] -> decode_syndrome  rounds=1
s[0:1] -> pauli_frame_update  X data[0:2]

machineRuns.title: A 4-qubit GHZ state
machineRuns.idea: A chain of CNOTs is the critical path; the four measurements then run in parallel, each on its own core.
machineRuns.source:
# A 4-qubit GHZ state: H, a chain of CNOTs, every qubit measured.
H  data[0]
CNOT  data[0], data[1]
CNOT  data[1], data[2]
CNOT  data[2], data[3]
measure  basis=Z  data[0] -> c[0]
measure  basis=Z  data[1] -> c[1]
measure  basis=Z  data[2] -> c[2]
measure  basis=Z  data[3] -> c[3]

machineRuns.title: Two rounds of the 3-qubit memory
machineRuns.idea: Ancillas are requested, measured and released every round; the second round's ancillas reuse the first round's transmons, and one decode reads both rounds.
machineRuns.source:
# Two rounds of the bit-flip code; each round takes fresh ancillas and returns them.
request_ancilla  count=2  ancilla[0:1]
CNOT  data[0], ancilla[0]
CNOT  data[1], ancilla[0]
CNOT  data[1], ancilla[1]
CNOT  data[2], ancilla[1]
measure  basis=Z  ancilla[0] -> s[0]
measure  basis=Z  ancilla[1] -> s[1]
release_ancilla  count=2  ancilla[0:1]
request_ancilla  count=2  ancilla[2:3]
CNOT  data[0], ancilla[2]
CNOT  data[1], ancilla[2]
CNOT  data[1], ancilla[3]
CNOT  data[2], ancilla[3]
measure  basis=Z  ancilla[2] -> s[2]
measure  basis=Z  ancilla[3] -> s[3]
release_ancilla  count=2  ancilla[2:3]
s[0:3] -> decode_syndrome  rounds=2
s[0:3] -> pauli_frame_update  X data[0:2]

studies.title: The classical fabric of a RISC-Q system
studies.summary: How long a measured bit takes to reach another core, how fast boards synchronize, and how many bits per microsecond a board and a lane between boards carry. Every system call that moves a classical bit pays these costs.

studies.title: decode_syndrome: a compiled decoder, calibrated
studies.summary: The decoder is a C program compiled for a RISC-Q core: union-find with peeling on each circuit's own detector graph (and cluster decoding with GF(2) elimination when the error model is a hypergraph). Its decode times are measured on noisy syndromes and become the system call's latency, its throughput and its decoding window.

studies.title: Every system call on six hardware designs
studies.summary: Eleven logical programs (memories, Deutsch–Jozsa, Bell pairs, a Z⊗Z merge, GHZ, a checked measurement, T injection, a loop of merges, at distances 3 and 5) on two designs of each platform. For every system call, the time each operation actually needed on the cycle-exact model, against the one number the machine declares.

studies.title: Magic-state factories under demand
studies.summary: A magic-state factory keeps only some of its attempts (postselection), so its output time is random. How many factories a stream of T gates needs, what a single factory latency misses, and who starves when requests have priorities.

studies.title: Decoder backlog: how many decoder cores
studies.summary: Each logical qubit produces a decoding job every few syndrome rounds. If the decoder is slower than the rounds, jobs queue and the backlog grows without bound. How many RISC-Q decoder cores keep up, against a count that reserves a decoder for the worst case of every decode.

studies.title: Deadlock and scheduling policy in a dynamic runtime
studies.summary: The resource VM admits a program as a fixed timetable. QuantumOS's runtime simulator instead runs the same program as soon as its dependencies and resources allow, the way a dynamic operating system would. Over the whole corpus: when does that deadlock, and how much faster is it when it does not?
